topic: The iPhone vs Android Upgrade Spiral
description: A chart-race of smartphone shipments and market share as Apple’s iPhone upgrade cycle turns into a global Android consolidation—then both collide again with the 2024–2025 slowdown.
youtube_description:
🎬 Timeline Comparison: The iPhone vs Android Upgrade Spiral

00:00 — The baseline: 2016–2017 momentum
00:25 — 2018–2019: iPhone stabilizes while the overall market tightens
01:00 — 2020 shock: supply chain disruption + demand shifts
01:35 — 2021 rebound: Apple pulls forward, Android regroups
02:05 — 2022 correction: global slowdown hits shipments
02:35 — 2023–2024 divergence: iPhone growth vs Android contraction
03:10 — 2025 plateau: upgrade cycles mature, total market flattens

The visual story here isn’t just “iPhone up, Android down.” It’s the upgrade spiral: Apple’s annual refresh cadence and premium installed-base pull iPhone shipments forward, while Android’s broad OEM base feels the macro slowdown harder—then both start moving more like the same market in 2024–2025.

instagram_caption:
🚀 The “upgrade spiral” that flipped the smartphone game—here’s how iPhone surged while Android quietly consolidated.

In 2016, the world was buying smartphones at a fast pace: **1,771M total units** shipped. **iPhone took 211M**, while the rest of the ecosystem—**Android**—moved **1,560M**. It looked like a simple story: Android had the volume, Apple had the premium. But the next few years rewrote the momentum.

By **2017**, total shipments rose to **1,846M**. iPhone edged to **216M**, while Android climbed to **1,630M**. Then in **2018**, the market peaked at **1,945M**. iPhone hit **225M**, showing Apple could keep pulling upgrade demand forward—refresh cycles and installed base turning into measurable shipment gravity.

The turning point hits in **2019–2020**. Total market dipped from **1,896M (2019)** to **1,953M (2020)**—a supply-and-demand jolt year. iPhone fell from **206M to 193M**, and Android swung from **1,690M to 1,760M**. Then **2021** delivered the dramatic rebound: total shipments jumped to **2,086M**. iPhone climbed to **226M**, while Android rose more modestly to **1,860M**. Translation: upgrades concentrated where demand was “sticky.”

Now watch what happens in the slowdown era. In **2022**, total shipments corrected to **1,888M**. iPhone held at **218M**, but Android dropped to **1,670M**. By **2023**, iPhone accelerated to **234M** while Android fell to **1,580M**—and the total market kept sliding to **1,814M**. In **2024**, iPhone continued rising to **238M**, while Android eased to **1,520M**. By **2025**, the total market flattens at **1,730M**: iPhone at **240M**, Android at **1,490M**.

So the real spiral isn’t just who “wins.” It’s how upgrade cycles change with macro pressure.

💬 What do you think is driving it more right now: **iPhone upgrade momentum** or **Android market consolidation**?

Smartphone competition increasingly behaves like an “upgrade spiral.” Using worldwide shipment totals to visualize the shift from broad Android volume toward steadier iPhone momentum, the chart shows a dramatic divergence during the 2022–2025 slowdown.

From 2016–2018, the market expanded from **1,771M to 1,945M** units. Apple’s iPhone shipments rose from **211M (2016)** to **225M (2018)**, while Android grew from **1,560M** to **1,720M**. In 2019–2020, total shipments were disrupted (down in 2019 to **1,896M**, then up in 2020 to **1,953M**), with iPhone moving **206M → 193M** and Android **1,690M → 1,760M**.

The divergence becomes clearer in the recovery and correction cycles. In 2021, total shipments jumped to **2,086M**; iPhone rebounded to **226M** and Android to **1,860M**. But when the slowdown hit, total shipments fell to **1,888M (2022)** and Android dropped sharply to **1,670M** while iPhone held near **218M**. By 2023–2025, iPhone increased from **234M (2023)** to **240M (2025)**, while Android slid from **1,580M (2023)** to **1,490M (2025)** as the total market flattened from **1,814M (2023)** to **1,730M (2025)**.

Bottom line: during weaker macro years, iPhone’s premium upgrade behavior shows up as shipment resilience, while Android’s broad OEM base becomes more sensitive to demand compression.
